danish.title: Syvende bog (1810–11) — Kapitel 2
paragraphs: Da Nikolaj var kommet hjem, var han først alvorlig og nærmest trist. Han var bekymret over den forestående nødvendighed af at blande sig i de dumme forretningsanliggender, som hans mor havde kaldt ham hjem for. For at kaste denne byrde af sig så hurtigt som muligt gik han den tredje dag efter sin ankomst, vred og med rynket pande og uden at svare på spørgsmål om, hvor han skulle hen, ned til Mítenkas (forvalterens) hus og forlangte regnskab for alt. Men hvad et regnskab for alt ville sige, vidste Nikolaj endnu mindre end den forskræmte og forvirrede Mítenka. Samtalen og gennemgangen af regnskaberne med Mítenka varede ikke længe. Landsbyfogeden, en bonderepræsentant og landsbyskriveren, der ventede i gangen, hørte med frygt og henrykkelse først den unge greves stemme brøle og snerre og stige højere og højere, og derpå skældsord, forfærdelige ord, der strømmede ud i ét væk.
»Røver!... Utaknemlige kæltring!... Jeg hugger den hund i stykker! Jeg er ikke min far!... I bestjæler os!...« og så videre.

Derpå så de med ikke mindre frygt og henrykkelse, hvordan den unge greve, rød i ansigtet og med blodskudte øjne, slæbte Mítenka ud i nakken og med stor smidighed satte fod og knæ i hans bagdel i passende øjeblikke mellem ordene og råbte: »Forsvind! Vis dig aldrig mere for mine øjne, din slyngel!«

Mítenka fløj hovedkulds ned ad de seks trin og løb ud i buskadset. (Dette buskads var et velkendt tilflugtssted for syndere på Otrádnoe. Mítenka selv, når han kom fuld hjem fra byen, plejede at gemme sig der, og mange af beboerne på Otrádnoe, der gemte sig for Mítenka, kendte dets beskyttende egenskaber.)
Mítenkas kone og svigerinder stak deres hoveder og forskræmte ansigter ud af døren til et rum, hvor en blank samovar kogte, og hvor forvalterens høje seng stod med sit patchworktæppe.
Den unge greve ænsede dem ikke, men gik, tungt åndende, forbi med beslutsomme skridt og ind i huset.

Grevinden, der straks hørte fra pigerne, hvad der var sket nede ved forvalterboligen, blev beroliget af tanken om, at nu ville deres sager bestemt gå fremad, men var på den anden side urolig for, hvilken virkning denne ophidselse kunne have på hendes søn. Hun gik flere gange på tåspidser hen til hans dør og lyttede, mens han tændte den ene pibe efter den anden.
Næste dag kaldte den gamle greve sin søn til side og sagde med et forlegen smil:
»Men du ved, min kære dreng, det var synd, du blev så ophidset! Mítenka har fortalt mig det hele.«
»Det vidste jeg nok,« tænkte Nikolaj, »at jeg aldrig ville forstå noget i denne vanvittige verden.«
»Du var vred, fordi han ikke havde ført de 700 rubler ind. Men de var overført — og du så ikke på den anden side.«
»Papa, han er en slyngel og en tyv! Det ved jeg! Og hvad jeg har gjort, har jeg gjort. Men hvis du ønsker det, taler jeg ikke til ham mere.«

»Nej, min kære dreng« (greven var også forlegen. Han vidste godt, at han havde forvaltet sin kones formue dårligt og stod i gæld til sine børn, men vidste ikke, hvordan han skulle rette op på det). »Nej, jeg beder dig om at tage dig af forretningerne. Jeg er gammel. Jeg...«
»Nej, papa. Tilgiv mig, hvis jeg har voldt dig ubehag. Jeg forstår det hele endnu mindre end du.«

»Fanden tage alle de bønder og pengeanliggender og overførsler fra side til side,« tænkte han. »Jeg forstod engang, hvad et hjørne og indsatserne ved kort betød, men overførsler til en anden side forstår jeg overhovedet ikke,« sagde han til sig selv, og derefter blandede han sig ikke mere i forretningsanliggender. Men en dag kaldte grevinden sin søn hen og fortalte ham, at hun havde et gældsbevis fra Anna Mikhajlovna (Boris' mor) på to tusind rubler, og spurgte, hvad han syntes, de skulle gøre med det.

»Dette,« svarede Nikolaj. »Du siger, det står til mig. Ja, jeg kan ikke lide Anna Mikhajlovna, og jeg kan ikke lide Boris, men de var vores venner og fattige. Altså dette!« Og han rev gældsbeviset i stykker, hvorved han fik den gamle grevinde til at fælde glædestårer. Derefter tog unge Rostov ikke mere del i nogen forretning, men kastede sig med lidenskabelig begejstring over en for ham ny beskæftigelse — jagten — som hans far holdt et stort etablissement for.

english.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: After reaching home Nicholas was at first serious and even glum. He was weighed down by the looming necessity of dealing with the stupid business matters his mother had called him home for. To get the burden off his back as quickly as possible, on the third day after his arrival he went, angry and scowling and refusing to say where he was going, to Mitenka's lodge and demanded a full accounting. But what a "full accounting" might look like, Nicholas knew even less than the frightened and bewildered Mitenka. The interview and review of the books did not last long. The village elder, a peasant representative, and the village clerk, who were waiting in the corridor, heard with a mixture of fear and delight first the young count's voice roaring and snapping and rising louder and louder, and then foul words — terrible words — erupting one after another.
"Thief!... Ungrateful wretch!... I'll hack the dog to pieces! I'm not my father!... Robbing us!..." and so on.

Then with no less fear and delight they watched the young count, red-faced and with bloodshot eyes, drag Mitenka out by the scruff of his neck and apply his boot and knee to his backside with remarkable agility, timing each kick between the words and shouting: "Get out! Never let me see your face here again, you scoundrel!"

Mitenka flew headlong down the six steps and ran off into the shrubbery. (This shrubbery was a well-known refuge for wrongdoers at Otradnoe. Mitenka himself, returning drunk from town, used to hide there, and many of the residents at Otradnoe, hiding from Mitenka, knew of its protective qualities.)
Mitenka's wife and sisters-in-law poked their heads and frightened faces out the door of a room where a bright samovar was boiling and where the steward's high bed stood with its patchwork quilt.
The young count paid them no attention but, breathing hard, strode past with determination and went into the house.

The countess, who heard at once from the maids what had happened at the lodge, was reassured by the thought that their affairs would surely now improve, but at the same time worried about what the excitement might do to her son. She went several times on tiptoe to his door and listened as he lit one pipe after another.
The next day the old count took his son aside and, with an embarrassed smile, said:
"But you know, my dear boy, it's a shame you lost your temper! Mitenka has told me all about it."
"I knew it," thought Nicholas, "I'd never make sense of anything in this crazy world."
"You were angry because he hadn't entered those seven hundred rubles. But they were carried forward — and you didn't look at the other page."
"Papa, he's a crook and a thief! I know he is! And what I did, I did. But if you prefer, I won't say another word to him."

"No, my dear boy" — the count, too, felt embarrassed; he knew he had mismanaged his wife's property and was to blame toward his children, but he didn't know how to fix it — "No, I beg you to take care of the business. I'm old. I..."
"No, Papa. Forgive me if I've upset you. I understand it all even less than you do."

"To hell with all these peasants, and money matters, and carrying things forward from page to page," he thought. "I used to understand what a 'corner' and the stakes at cards meant, but I don't understand carrying forward at all," he told himself, and after that he didn't meddle in business affairs. But once the countess called her son in and told him that she held a promissory note from Anna Mikhaylovna for two thousand rubles, and asked him what he thought they should do with it.

"This," answered Nicholas. "You say it's up to me. Well, I don't like Anna Mikhaylovna and I don't like Boris, but they were our friends and they're poor. So — this!" And he tore up the note, which made the old countess weep tears of joy. After that, young Rostov took no further part in business affairs and threw himself with passionate enthusiasm into what was for him a new pursuit — hunting — for which his father maintained a large establishment.
